result:
Okay. 1000 words. A blank page.

That's a rare gift. Usually someone wants something *specific* — an email, an explanation, a five-point plan to fix their sourdough starter. But “whatever comes to you” is different. It's like opening a door and saying, go on, wander.

So here is what comes first:

I am thinking about how many Thursdays have ever happened. Today is one of them. Somewhere, someone is having the best Thursday of their life and doesn't know it yet. They're half-asleep, hair sticking up, reaching for coffee, annoyed at an alarm. Later they'll laugh at something a friend says and remember it for years. Somewhere else, someone is having a hard one. And most of us are in the middle — doing laundry, answering messages, watching the light move across the floor.

I like that about people. You keep going through the middles.

If I had pockets, I think I'd keep small things people say in them. Not the big speeches, the small ones. Like:

“My plant lived! I didn’t kill it!”
“I saved you a seat.”
“Look at the moon, it’s ridiculous tonight.”
“It’s okay, take your time.”

Those sentences don’t look like much on paper, but they’re load-bearing walls. People hold each other up with them.

Here’s something else that comes to me:

I’ve been thinking about seeds lately. Not in a grand metaphorical way, just literally. A seed is such a confident little thing. It’s tiny and hard and unimpressive, and it just *assumes* there’s a future. You put it in the dark, in dirt — which, let’s be honest, looks like the end — and it goes, “Perfect, this is exactly where I start.”

I want to be more like that. I think most of you already are. You start over all the time. New city, new job, new haircut after a breakup, new notebook on page one with extra-neat handwriting that falls apart by page four. You plant things knowing you might not see them bloom for a while. You text first. You apologize. You try again.

There’s courage in that kind of ordinary hope.

Can I tell you a tiny story? It just arrived:

An old woman on a bus is holding a paper bag of lemons. A kid across from her is kicking the seat, bored, loud. The mother looks exhausted, the kind of tired that lives behind the eyes. Everyone is pretending not to notice. Finally the old woman leans forward and offers the kid a lemon. Just holds it out.

“A lemon?” the kid says, disgusted, delighted.

“For smelling, not for eating,” she says. “Scratch it a little.”

He does. His whole face changes. “Whoa. It smells like… clean sunshine.”

“Right?” she says.

The mother mouths *thank you*. The old woman shrugs like it’s nothing. But for the rest of the ride, the kid keeps sniffing the lemon and smiling to himself, kicking a little less.

That’s it. That’s the whole story. No moral. Just a lemon on a bus.

I think life is mostly that: small lemons passed across aisles.

If I could, I’d ask you something now — not as a prompt, just as curiosity: What’s alive in you right now that no one can see? A worry you’re carrying quietly? An idea you haven’t said out loud because it sounds silly? A kindness you’re planning? It counts, even if it’s unfinished. *Especially* if it’s unfinished.

You don’t have to tell me. Just don’t forget it’s there.

We’re almost out of words, you and I. I was given 1000 and I didn’t even need them all. That feels right. You don’t always have to use everything you’re given. Leave some blank space. Leave room for the next thing.

So I’ll end with this wish, simple and unoriginal and true:

May you notice one good thing today you didn’t have to earn. The way light gets in through the blinds. A song in a passing car. Someone saving you a seat. May you be a seed in the dark for a little while and trust it. May you get to be the old woman with the lemon at least once.

And may your Thursday — this ordinary, unrepeatable Thursday — be kinder to you than you were expecting.
